articles.title_orig: Georgia and China: Han Zheng’s Visit to Tbilisi as Strategic Signalling
articles.title_zh: Georgia and China: Han Zheng’s Visit to Tbilisi as Strategic Signalling
articles.content_orig:
The recent visit of Chinese Vice President Han Zheng to Georgia confirms Beijing’s interest in, and strategic approach to, the South Caucasus, as well as Tbilisi’s need to attract foreign investors in order to build a logistics role in the Black Sea region and along the Middle Corridor.
However, Tbilisi’s economic and political imperatives sit uneasily with its constraints, which include frozen relations with the European Union, dependence on Russian trade, narrow commercial opportunities and Black Sea security risks.
This report seeks to establish whether Han Zheng’s official visit should be read as a strong geopolitical signal, or whether it belongs more to the realm of strategic communication and narrative speculation.
On 6-8 November 2026 , Chinese Vice President Han Zheng is paying a historic three-day official visit to Tbilisi. He met President Mikheil Kavelashvili on the first day and is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze .
The two sides discussed the strategic partnership, the free trade agreement, growth in Chinese investment, the Middle Corridor and transport infrastructure, a sixth Silk Road Forum in Tbilisi, direct flights, tourism, education and a joint working group on artificial intelligence.
Kavelashvili thanked China for supporting his country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and reaffirmed Georgia’s One China position . He also proposed a global peace and healthy lifestyle summit in Tbilisi in 2027 and asked for Chinese participation.
On 9 June 1992, the two countries established diplomatic relations and declared a strategic partnership in July 2023. On 9 June 2026 , Xi Jinping and Kavelashvili announced a further upgrade of bilateral relations on the occasion of the 34th anniversary of diplomatic ties.
Kobakhidze stated in August 2026 that China is Georgia’s third-largest trading partner and second-largest market for its domestic exports , and that visa-free travel, expanded direct flights and a Tbilisi-Shanghai route support tourism, business and investment. Shanghai and Tbilisi established friendly exchange ties in 2025.
Han Zheng’s official visit occurs in a period of deteriorated relations between Georgia and the European Union . In 2024 , Tbilisi announced the suspension of EU accession talks until 2028, although the Georgian government described this decision as a halt, not an abandonment.
On 8 October 2026 , the European Parliament adopted a resolution condemning the ruling Georgian Dream party’s attempts to ban opposition parties and calling for sanctions against senior officials, naming Bidzina Ivanishvili, Kobakhidze, Shalva Papuashvili and Kakha Kaladze as targets for sanctions and visa bans. The EU has already suspended visa-free travel for holders of Georgian diplomatic passports, and a European Commission report warns that all Georgian citizens could lose visa-free access.
Georgia’s central imperative is to attract investors and turn its geography into a logistics role linking East and West through the Middle Corridor. The Middle Corridor is significant to Tbilisi’s national agenda because it connects China and Europe while bypassing Russia.
The South Caucasus republic’s logistics potential faces four constraints that investors and policymakers need to address:
China’s interests are narrower : Beijing receives an explicit Georgian reaffirmation of its One China position and a transit partner on the Middle Corridor, while Georgia receives public Chinese support for its territorial integrity, a point of value given Abkhazia and South Ossetia. The visit gives Tbilisi a counterweight to Brussels in public messaging.
Despite Han Zheng’s official visit and Beijing’s opportunity to invest in the Georgian market, the European Union still holds the instruments that matter to Georgia , namely candidate status, visa-free access and sanctions decisions, and China offers no substitute for any of them. The European Parliament and the Commission acted on Georgia in the weeks before the visit, which shows no sign that Brussels reads closer Chinese ties as a cost to be reduced.
Conversely, deeper Chinese engagement in Georgia could make Tbilisi more dependent on Beijing’s decisions, given that the US Helsinki Commission has already voiced concern about Chinese control and dominance in the Black Sea region.
Russia , for its part, could interpret major Chinese involvement in the Georgian market and, by extension, in the South Caucasus as a warning sign for its own logistics projects, since Beijing’s strategy might bypass the Russian corridor.
The visit can be ascribed to the fields of strategic communication and foreign relations, since the parties discussed the basis for further work without reaching a substantive commitment. The outcome of the visit therefore depends on whether Chinese involvement in Georgia’s strategic infrastructure becomes consistent.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot to be tasked with forming next Israeli government
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot to be tasked with forming next Israeli government
articles.content_orig:
In a setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his main rival will be tasked with forming the next Israeli government, placing him one step closer to ousting Israel’s longest-serving leader, even as the path remains complicated.
Gadi Eisenkot, a retired military chief who led the centrist Yashar party in the October 27 election, will have up to six weeks to try and assemble a coalition to replace Netanyahu. But his path to power is fraught with political obstacles and divisions within the opposition itself.
President Isaac Herzog will officially give Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on Sunday, his office said in a statement. Herzog’s decision followed two days of consultations last week with all parties elected to the Knesset.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Believes Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Had a Relationship With a Suspected Chinese Spy
articles.title_zh: U.S. Believes Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Had a Relationship With a Suspected Chinese Spy
articles.content_orig:
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
He runs the most powerful A.I. company in the world, and now the U.S. government believes he was romantically involved with a Chinese spy: According to the Financial Times , U.S. officials believe that Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at the Nvidia customer Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence believes she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security. For Nvidia, worth more than $4 trillion on the stock market, the case has become a problem at the very top.
The report is based on a memo that U.S. officials wrote earlier this year, drawing on information obtained by American intelligence, the FT said. The memo said Mr. Huang had been romantically involved with Alice Huang. The two are not related. It was shared with a small group of top U.S. government officials shortly before President Trump traveled to Beijing in May for a summit with Xi Jinping. The White House and the C.I.A. declined to comment. Photographs and videos showing the two together have circulated on social media.
On Friday, The New York Times reported that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, worked directly for China’s top spy agency. Her tasks reportedly included persuading the Nvidia chief to lobby for exports of advanced chips to China. The operation dates back to at least 2024, according to The Times. In late October, the newspaper first reported that U.S. intelligence considered the Megaspeed executive a source for Beijing and that she had been in close contact with Jensen Huang .
Megaspeed, based in Singapore, was spun off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023. It is suspected of smuggling advanced Nvidia chips into China in violation of U.S. export controls. Nvidia conducted an internal review of the allegations and found no evidence of wrongdoing. The U.S. government has been investigating companies, particularly in Southeast Asia, that are believed to be funneling chips to China. Washington’s concern is that advanced A.I. chips could speed up China’s military modernization.
The case is all the more sensitive because Mr. Huang personally lobbied Mr. Trump earlier this year to let Nvidia sell its H200 chips in China . According to the FT, U.S. national security officials have privately expressed frustration with the Nvidia chief.
Mr. Huang has met with Mr. Trump several times since the president began his second term. An episode from May shows how close the two are: When Mr. Trump flew to China for the summit, Mr. Huang was not initially among the chief executives aboard Air Force One. When the president learned of this, he called Mr. Huang personally, according to the FT. The Nvidia chief then flew to Alaska and boarded the presidential plane during a stopover. In September, he attended the state dinner Mr. Trump held for Mr. Xi during his visit to the United States.
Now the case has reached Congress. Top Republican lawmakers have asked Mr. Huang to appear in private before the House committees on China, foreign affairs and intelligence. They want to ask him about the alleged spying operation and about Nvidia’s security protocols. According to The Times, a closed-door briefing is planned for mid-November.
Nothing has been proved so far, and all of the information comes from anonymous sources. Nvidia declined to comment on the memo or on the assertion that its chief executive had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang. The company has previously said that Mr. Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year.” John Rizzo, an Nvidia spokesman, told The Times that the company does not share classified information with customers and that the interactions were “not unusual.” Alice Huang could not be reached for comment. The Chinese Embassy in Washington called the reports unsubstantiated and “nothing but smears against China.”

articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.content_orig:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".
In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.
At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.
No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.
Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.
"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.
He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids â any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".
Thomas Markle appeared in court on Friday
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.
The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.
In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

articles.title_zh: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.content_orig:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has now recorded 5,182 measles cases in the U.S. in 2026 â the highest number of cases since 1991 .
The latest CDC figures , published Friday, said there were 5,164 measles cases across 45 states and D.C., with a further 18 cases recorded affecting international visitors.
Measles â which was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 â is caused by a virus that is among the worldâs most contagious pathogens.
Declining vaccination rates have left growing numbers of children and adults susceptible to the virus, with multiple states experiencing sustained outbreaks of the disease.
On Monday, it was reported that a child had died in New Yorkâs Lewis County â the first such death in the state in 30 years. On Wednesday , Pennsylvania reported its sixth measles-related death of the year. And on Thursday state officials announced an infant had died in Wisconsin.
The Johns Hopkins Universityâs measles tracker had recorded 5,400 cases in the U.S. as of Friday. Their data is based on information that is scraped from state and county health departments, along with other resources, so its figures are ahead of reports from the CDC.
Of all the places that got swept up in the Democratic âblue wave,â one of the most unlikely was the heart of the Venezuelan diaspora in the U.S.
Doral, a city in South Florida often called âDoralzuelaâ for its large concentration of Venezuelan immigrants, shifted 14 points from 2024 to narrowly back Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon. Nixon, a progressive state lawmaker, fell short in her challenge to Sen. Ashley Moody (R).
The results in Doral â the largest swing in Miami-Dade County â are remarkable in a community of Venezuelan immigrants who fled a socialist strongman.
Trump won a commanding victory in Doral two years ago thanks to his promise to oust Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro. After the U.S. military seized Maduro and his wife in January, crowds celebrated in the streets of Doral.
Other Trump initiatives appear to have pulled Venezuelans toward Democrats, a signal the GOPâs grip on Venezuelan-American voters is not impenetrable.
The administration in early 2025 stripped hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans of a temporary legal status that protects them from deportation. More recently, immigration agents have targeted the Miami suburb, which is also home to a Trump golf club.
âWe hear our community,â Doral Mayor Christi Fraga (R) said in a statement. âPeople are frustrated, and those concerns should not be dismissed. I believe this is an important moment for the Republican Party to listen, reflect, and get to work on these issues.â
New Zealandâs general election remains too close to call, with both major parties currently neck-and-neck at 29.21% and 29.36%.
The vote had been dubbed the â battle of the Chrises ,â with incumbent Christopher Luxon of the center-right National Party, and leader of the opposition center-left Labour Party Chris Hipkins, competing to become prime minister.
Hundreds of thousands of â special votes â â including from those casting ballots from overseas - are still to be counted and could be decisive in determining which party is able to form a path to government.
A significant number of voters have supported minor parties, including Opportunity, a centrist party led by Qiulae Wong, a Fiji-born former consultant who only entered politics a year ago after seeing an ad seeking applicants to head the party.
Hipkins said Saturday: âTonight, New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that youâve said.â
Luxon told supporters it appeared they would be the largest party in Parliament, but the final results were still âtoo close to call.â
He congratulated his rivals on a âhard-fought race,â and admonished a supporter who appeared to boo, saying: âWe donât do that here - itâs not the Kiwi way.â
A YouGov poll conducted one day after Democratsâ sweeping midterm victories asked whether the results were more a reflection of âvotersâ opinions of Donald Trump,â âvotersâ opinions of the candidates on the ballotâ or âboth equally.â Far more Americans said Trump was a bigger factor than candidates on the ballot â 38 percent vs. 11 percent â while 32 percent said the results reflected opinions about both Trump and the candidates.
Reactions were similar among Republicans, with 36 percent saying the election results reflected opinions about Trump, 16 percent saying the results reflected views about candidates on the ballot, and 31 percent saying Trump and the candidates were equal factors.
Those reactions suggest most Republicans hold Trump solely or partly responsible for their partyâs midterm losses, a perception that could undermine his influence in the GOP going forward.
Less than a month before the midterms, 61 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents said the GOPâs leaders should âfollow Trumpâs leadership,â while 37 percent said they should go in a âdifferent direction,â according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll .
State and city officials in Pennsylvania are condemning as antisemitic a planned bike protest in Philadelphia urging boycotts of a half-dozen Jewish-owned restaurants.
The event called for noon Sunday is being organized, according to local station WPVI-TV, by several groups, including Philly Bike On Your Left.
Officials and critics say the businesses are being targeted because they are owned by Jews, and are lambasting ride organizers.
Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) said in a statement Thursday that the bike ride âmasquerading as a protest to advance the cause of justice, is nothing more than blatant antisemitism designed to intimidate and drive Jewish businesses out of our communities.â
Attorney General Dave Sunday called the event âunconscionableâ in a statement . He noted that the protest will happen a day before the anniversary of Kristallnacht, a massive, deadly state-approved 1938 pogrom in Nazi Germany and Austria against synagogues and Jewish businesses.
Ride organizers referred WPVI-TV to a statement by a group calling for a boycott of restaurants owned by the group CookNSolo, which focuses on Israeli cuisine. The statement said that one of the restaurant groupâs owners has partnered with the Israeli Ministry of Tourism and that several restaurants hosted free events for Israeli soldiers, among other reasons.
A call for comment to CookNSolo wasnât immediately returned Friday.
The ride organizersâ statement also said âZionists have mounted a coordinated campaign to discredit and villainize the organizers and detract from their anti-genocide message.â Criticsâ references to Kristallnacht are âcynical,â the statement added.
In the blue tide overtaking the country this week, Alabama voters elected the first openly gay sheriff as well as the stateâs first openly transgender legislator.
Democrat Brett Jones, in Madison County, defeated a two-term Republican incumbent to take over the law enforcement role. Jones is a former Navy SEAL who wrote a 2014 book about his experience of being gay in the military called âPride: The Story of the First Openly Gay Navy SEAL.â
Jones, a police officer at the University of Alabama at Huntsville, campaigned on transparency, jail reform and discontinuing the countyâs contract with Flock, the controversial license plate reader system that has sparked widespread concern about overreaching government surveillance .
âMy being gay has absolutely nothing to do with how Iâm going to do my job,â Jones told reporters in Alabama this week. âMy job is to reform that jail and respect peopleâs constitutional rights.â
Voters also chose Allison Montgomery, a software engineer and civil rights advocate, as the first openly transgender person elected to the Alabama state legislature.

articles.title_zh: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.content_orig:
Late night political drama as PeÃ±a is impeached and arrested
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago PeÃ±a over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
PeÃ±a, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Pedro Alliana takes the oath of office as interim President
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.content_orig:
John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft.
He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg , which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. 6.
The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September.
Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported.
His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned.
Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT.
Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably.
Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks.
Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger.
Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data.
He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported.
Those are his judgments. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy.
Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side.
Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal.
He doubted research could reach use from there either.
Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use.
He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg.
His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library.
A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader.
Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft.
It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions.
It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic.
The link is unproven. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.

US officials are presenting a list of topics, including security guarantees and European security architecture, for upcoming negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, as issues that the United States, Europe, Ukraine, and Russia agree to discuss. Russia’s frequently reiterated positions on these topics, however, remain incompatible with the official positions and interests of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe. Former Senior Advisor to the US President Jared Kushner stated on November 5 that a US delegation held “productive” talks with Ukrainian, NATO, and European partners in Brussels to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and the broader European security architecture as part of a lasting peace in Ukraine.[1] Kushner added that the United States is exploring five principal goals to address all parties’ security concerns through mutually agreed agreements: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.[2] Kushner stated that NATO will remain central to Europe’s collective defense and that each state will retain the authority to make decisions about its alliances–presumably referring to the rights of Ukraine to continue its aspirations to join NATO and of current NATO member states to remain part of the alliance. Kushner also noted that the United States aims to move to a broader multilateral negotiation format with direct European participation should the upcoming trilateral US-Ukrainian-Russian November 10-11 talks in Abu Dhabi make progress.
Russian demands for ending its war in Ukraine undermine wider US policy objectives relating to Europe’s defense and contradict Ukrainian and European negotiating positions. The Kremlin recently reiterated its 2021 demand that NATO roll back to its 1997 borders, contradicting Kushner’s statement about NATO’s role in Europe’s defense and individual states’ decision-making power about alliances.[3] This Russian demand also conflicts with US President Donald Trump’s ongoing efforts to establish a US Army base in Poland.[4] Moscow’s position on security guarantees for Ukraine has also long differed from that of Europe and Ukraine, with Russia repeatedly rejecting any possibility of the deployment of foreign forces to Ukraine and discussing having Russia and China involved in guaranteeing Ukraine’s security.[5] Kremlin officials have also revived their demand that European officials not be able to participate in negotiations to end the war so long as they refuse to negotiate on Russian terms.[6] Although US, European, Ukrainian, and Russian officials all seem to agree on the need to discuss the European security architecture as part of the peace settlement, the Russian position is incompatible with that of European and Ukrainian officials and with the requirements for establishing and maintaining durable peace both in Ukraine and Europe.
An unidentified actor is conducting a coordinated campaign of hoax bomb threats targeting European commercial flights, airports, and media outlets, likely to disrupt European society and impose economic costs. One or more unidentified actors issued bomb threats to at least 18 commercial planes and airports on November 6, bringing the total number of bomb threats against European aviation during the week of November 2 to over 50.[7] An anonymous senior broadcaster from Irish media outlet RTÉ stated that an unidentified actor issued bomb threats to 18 media organizations on November 6.[8] RTÉ, Irish media outlet Newstalk, Bulgarian media outlet Nova TV, and UK media outlet Sky News confirmed that they received threats.[9] A “Mikhail Andropov” signed the bomb threat message, titled “Message to the West,” sent to various European news outlets on November 6 and claimed responsibility for the previous hoax bomb threats against European commercial flights since November 2.[10] RTÉ and Newstalk stated that “Mikhail Andropov” claimed to be preparing a “new wave of attacks” over an unspecified period.[11] Reuters reported that it was unable to establish the sender’s identity, the email’s origin, or whether the email originated from the same source as the threats to any or all of the commercial planes affected during the week of November 2.[12] European security services effectively and promptly responded to the bomb threats, including by scrambling NATO aircraft to escort some of the threatened commercial planes, and did not find explosives in any of the targeted aircraft, airports, or newsrooms.[13]
European states have not yet attributed this coordinated campaign to a specific actor, but it advances the Kremlin’s military and cognitive campaigns against Europe and is consistent with Russian approaches, which ISW assessed in two papers published in September 2026. [14] European leaders, including Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto and Irish Taoiseach (head of the national government) Micheál Martin separately described the spate of recent bomb threats as “coordinated” in statements on November 5 and 6.[15] Irish Member of the European Parliament Barry Andrews stated “it is not a coincidence, in my mind, that this occurs days before Ireland hosts a major summit, hosting over 50 leaders,” noting that two informal EU summits are set to take place in Dublin, Ireland during the week of November 9.[16] European leaders should continue to prioritize attributing kinetic attacks and other threats to Russia or other responsible actors once they have gathered sufficient evidence to do so, as the German government did on September 1 following the Russian sabotage attack against Leipzig Halle airport on August 4.[17]
The Russian government continues to reduce its civil servants’ staffing level in order to cut non-essential social spending amid rising budget deficits. Russian State Duma sources told Russian business outlet RBK on November 5 that the State Duma will reduce its workforce by approximately 15 to 20 percent and that the Russian Federation Council will reduce its staff by approximately 10 to 15 percent.[18] Sources stated that the reduction of government staffing levels is aimed at reducing government spending and that there will be no “drastic cuts,” as Russian authorities will likely eliminate unstaffed positions and lay off retirement-age employees first. RBK noted that Russian authorities will shrink the State Duma and Federation Council based on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s October 2024 decree that calls for a reduction of at least 10 percent in civil servant numbers within some government agencies to pay bonuses to employees of relevant government agencies.[19] Moscow City Mayor Sergei Sobyanin in March 2026 similarly reduced the number of civil servants in Moscow City’s executive and administrative agencies by 15 percent due to Moscow City’s slowing budget revenue growth.[20] The State Duma and Federation Council staff cuts are the latest examples of the Kremlin’s ongoing efforts to cut non-essential social spending to direct more government funds toward Russia’s war efforts in Ukraine.[21]

articles.title_orig: Police Probe German Man After Teen Is Stranded on Mountain
articles.title_zh: Police Probe German Man After Teen Is Stranded on Mountain
articles.content_orig:
Austrian police are investigating a German man aged 21 on suspicion of endangering public safety, after his 17-year-old female friend was left stranded on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze in sub-zero temperatures.
The teenager called emergency services and was eventually rescued on the mountain at an altitude of about 2,500m (8,200ft).
She was suffering from hypothermia and taken to hospital in nearby Garmisch-Partenkirchen, over the border in Germany, before being discharged.
In Austria, anyone who endangers another person's physical safety can be punished with up to three months in prison.
The pair set off in the early hours of Sunday from the resort of Ehrwald in the Austrian Tyrol with the aim of seeing the sunrise on Zugspitze.
Temperatures that morning had fallen to -12C, a mountain rescuer told German Press Agency DPA.
The weather was so poor that the two climbers were soon knee-deep in snow, according to Austrian reports, and their plans to reach the 2,962m summit soon changed.
At one point they separated and the 21-year-old descended alone. The reason they split is unclear, and a police spokesperson declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.
Seven mountain rescuers responded to the call, and a helicopter eventually airlifted the teenager off the mountain. She was then taken to hospital by ambulance.
Although the teenager survived, what happened on Zugspitze on Sunday is reminiscent of a fatal incident on Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner, in January 2025.
A 33-year-old woman froze to death on the Grossglockner after her boyfriend left her on the mountain, and he was later found guilty of grossly negligent manslaughter.
The boyfriend had insisted he had left her there while trying to get help, telling the court he had loved his girlfriend and that he was deeply sorry.
The case reverberated throughout the mountaineering community at the time, with prosecutors arguing that as the more experienced climber, he was the responsible guide on the trip and had failed to turn back or call for help in time.
In the latest case in Austria, police have said once they have completed their investigation, a report will be sent to Innsbruck public prosecutors, who will decide if a criminal offence has been committed.

articles.title_orig: Airline begins charging $140 for checked bags on some roundtrip flights
articles.title_zh: Airline begins charging $140 for checked bags on some roundtrip flights
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to the era of the $70 bag fee.
JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits.
Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure.
There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status.
"We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement. "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
The price of jet fuel, airlines' biggest cost after labor, has roughly doubled this year since the start of the Iran war in February, costing airlines billions and driving up the price of tickets. Jet fuel was going for $4.44 a gallon on Tuesday for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Other airlines often follow when one carrier raises fees. Major U.S. airlines did so earlier this year after JetBlue raised its bag fees.
The changes were reported earlier by the Thrifty Traveler blog .

articles.title_orig: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.title_zh: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6's PS5 Physical Edition Revealed in First Photo
articles.title_zh: GTA 6's PS5 Physical Edition Revealed in First Photo
articles.content_orig:
Images of GTA 6’s physical edition have emerged on Reddit , ahead of its release later in the month.
The anticipated open world game – which won’t include a disc – looks practically identical to every other PS5 release, in a sealed blue plastic case with the usual logos and layout.
While this is a German copy, there’s a disclaimer on the front which mentions no disc is included, and only a download code is packaged inside.
The photos, first shared on Reddit but since deleted, have been reposted below:
Fans will be able to purchase boxed versions of the Rockstar release from retailers starting 12th November, allowing a week for them to pre-load the 212GB title ahead of launch .
This is the first major title to ship in a “code-in-box” format, although it will become a lot more common in 2028, when Sony’s signalled its intent to cease manufacturing Blu-ray discs .
Personally, I’m concerned about the waste of plastic here. I understand some people may still want a case to display with their other games, but if we’re getting rid of discs, I’d like Sony to implement some sort of recyclable format moving forward.
Remember, if you want a map of Leonidas to go with your physical copy of GTA 6, you’ll need to purchase that separately for $0.99 from the Rockstar Store.
You can find out more information about GTA 6’s pre-load through here .
In the meantime, do let me know if any of you are planning to purchase the physical version and why below.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.content_orig:
Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media that Russia used 36 missiles to target critical infrastructure. Only four missiles were taken down, Zelenskyy said, highlighting a shortage of interceptors . He also said 172 drones were used in the attacks, which struck Kyiv and 12 other regions.
The president accused Russia of intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and the country's infrastructure ahead of trilateral talks .
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration , the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
"Russia has a very particular view of diplomacy – as a subtype of aggression," Zelenskyy wrote.
"We hope that the United States, like our other partners, will act on principle," he added.
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages , national and city authorities said.
Zelenskyy said a kindergarten was "partially destroyed." Photos show rubble near the damaged building.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.
"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"
Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 892-yard-long Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River. Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."
Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.
Russia also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.
Zelenskyy said that at one energy facility, preliminary findings show Russia used KN-23 missiles "manufactured and supplied by North Korea." He called the use of the alleged North Korean missile "further proof that global sanctions regimes need to be significantly strengthened." Technical assessments at other sites are ongoing.
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.
"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.
The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

articles.title_orig: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
articles.title_zh: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
articles.content_orig:
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen , a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence .
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz , a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal , a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron , a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson , a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

articles.title_orig: Millions of ladders recalled nationwide after numerous reports of head injuries, skull fractures
articles.title_zh: Millions of ladders recalled nationwide after numerous reports of head injuries, skull fractures
articles.content_orig:
Apothecary Pharma recalls compounded tirzepatide vials distributed nationwide due to sterility concerns. Ashley Webster reports on the FDA classification of the recall and the North Carolina company's production practices.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is recalling more than 3.6 million Little Giant ladders after receiving dozens of reports of injuries, including head trauma and skull fractures.
The ladders, according to the recall , have a mechanism called "Rapid Locks" that are designed to be inserted into the ladders' rungs to help adjust the height.
According to a statement from Little Giant, the Rapid Locks can fail to become fully engaged, causing the ladders to retract and posing a potential fall hazard to consumers.
The company has received 25 reports of the ladders retracting, 19 of which resulted in injury.
NEARLY 6 MILLION COFFEE MAKERS SOLD AT MAJOR RETAILERS RECALLED OVER BURN RISK
Recalled Little Giant Adjustable Fortress 2.0 ladder (Unknown)
Those incidents resulted in three reports of head injuries which, according to the recall, include traumatic brain injury, skull fractures, concussions, vision loss, hearing loss and cognitive impairment.
The company has also received 16 reports of other injuries such as joint or bone fractures, lacerations and bruising.
Overall, the company has received 39 reports of the Rapid Locks not working properly.
WALMART RECALLS 4.4 MILLION GRILL BRUSHES OVER SERIOUS INJURY RISK
Recalled Little Giant Conquest 2.0 ladder (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission / Unknown)
The recall involves 11 makes of Little Giant's ladders and over 130 models ranging from $100 to $1,000.
Little Giant is adding supplemental warning labels to affected ladders, instructing users to visually verify that all Rapid Locks are fully engaged before climbing.
"You should stop using your ladder until you have received and applied the warning labels included in the repair kit according to the enclosed instructions, which contain further guidance on safely operating the Rapid Locks and maintaining the Rapid Locks with lubrication," Little Giant said in a statement announcing the recall.
The company is also sending repair kits to all known users with Rapid Locks malfunctions.
"The repair kit contains instructions, also accessible via the QR code on the ladder, for safely operating the Rapid Locks and maintaining the Rapid Locks with lubrication," the company added.
Recalled Little Giant Quantum ladder (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission / Unknown)
CPSC advised consumers to maintain the Little Giant ladders' Rapid Locks with lubrication and to evaluate their ladders on a regular basis.
"If a lock does not function properly after this evaluation, the company will offer the choice of a replacement ladder of the same or equivalent model or a refund ranging from a depreciated value determined by date of purchase up to full purchase price for ladders purchased within the past 12 months," CPSC said in the recall.

articles.title_orig: Why Italy’s Giorgia Meloni Is Willing to Lose Votes Over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Why Italy’s Giorgia Meloni Is Willing to Lose Votes Over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Giorgia Meloni wants EU leaders to decide who can speak for them in Ukraine peace talks. Her letter to António Costa reflects a position she took before entering office: Ukraine’s right to defend its independence matters to Italy’s own security, even when defending it costs her votes.
On Nov. 5, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni asked European Council President António Costa a question the European Union has left unanswered for far too long. Who has the authority to speak for the EU in negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine?
In her letter to Costa , Meloni pointed to a series of uncoordinated diplomatic initiatives, including individual European leaders holding talks with Vladimir Putin. She called for a decision at the December summit and made clear that she was seeking the role neither for herself nor for Italy. At a time when Moscow is counting on European divisions, the prime minister of one of the EU’s largest countries has asked her fellow leaders to agree on who speaks for them.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Four years ago, many expected Meloni herself to be the source of just such a division. Her party had roots in Italy’s post-fascist tradition, and her coalition partners gave her critics plenty of ammunition. Silvio Berlusconi spoke openly about his friendship with Putin. Matteo Salvini had spent years expressing sympathy for the Kremlin. The expectation was that, under Meloni, Italy would become the West’s weak link on Ukraine.
Meloni made her position clear before she even entered office. When Berlusconi sought to excuse Moscow’s invasion and attacked Volodymyr Zelensky in the autumn of 2022, she told him there would be no place in her government for parties that rejected Italy’s European and Atlantic commitments. She needed Berlusconi to form a coalition. Yet she chose Russia and Ukraine as the issue on which she would not compromise.
In doing so, Meloni posed a question to Europe’s right that many of its politicians would still prefer to avoid. If patriotism rests on a people’s right to determine its own future, what could be more patriotic than Ukraine’s resistance to Russian occupation? No one can credibly defend the sovereignty of their own country while accepting Russia’s supposed right to dictate a neighboring nation’s borders and government by force. Yet some European nationalists try to reconcile those positions by treating Moscow’s territorial demands as the basis for peace.
At the Crimea Platform summit on Aug. 23, 2023, Meloni reminded her audience that Russia’s aggression had begun in 2014, with the seizure of Crimea and the occupation of parts of the Donbas. She also acknowledged that Western governments had been wrong to assume Putin would stop there. After Crimea, major business deals continued, energy ties endured and diplomats tried to bring relations with Moscow back within acceptable bounds. Putin drew the lesson that military conquest could become an accepted political fact. Ukraine was left to live with the consequences.
“Your freedom is freedom for the whole of Europe,” Meloni told Ukrainians that day .
That argument has particular force for Italy. If Russia can force Ukraine to surrender territory and accept limits on its independence, the next European country it threatens will face a Kremlin with good reason to believe that aggression pays. Should that country be a NATO member, Italy and its allies would face a choice between a military response and abandoning their commitment to collective defense. Either would carry a grave cost. It is far wiser to prevent that dilemma while Ukrainians are still fighting the aggressor themselves.
Meloni is prepared to make that case to Italian voters. In September, she told Il Foglio that, in purely electoral terms, it would have been easier not to support Ukraine. Ahead of next year’s election, she ruled out an alliance with parties that vote against military aid for Kyiv .
Salvini opposes further arms deliveries, and some voters on the right want closer ties with Moscow and an end to sanctions. Every new package for Kyiv gives Meloni’s coalition partners an opportunity to reopen the argument. She has had ample opportunity to scale back assistance and spare herself the confrontation.
Instead, her government is preparing a 13th military assistance package for Kyiv . Italy has already supplied air defense equipment, and Defense Minister Guido Crosetto has said he will seek to extend the aid arrangements into 2027 despite opposition within the coalition. In 2025, Rome also hosted the Ukraine Recovery Conference , bringing governments, financial institutions and businesses together to plan for Ukraine’s reconstruction.
Putin’s strategy toward the West depends in part on the expectation that elections will eventually deliver what his army cannot. He has every interest in Italian politicians turning each shipment of air defense equipment into an argument about what it might cost them at the polls. Ukrainian families, meanwhile, are raising children for whom air-raid sirens are part of ordinary life. They know precisely what a shortage of air defenses can cost.
On Oct. 14, that same understanding of Italy’s interests put Meloni at odds with Donald Trump. Speaking in the Italian parliament, she called his agreement with Russia on diesel supplies a very risky decision. She warned that the deal could give Moscow additional revenue to finance its war, weaken sanctions and lend Russia legitimacy while Russian bombs continued to fall on Ukrainian cities.
Meloni shares much of Trump’s conservative outlook and has invested in good relations with his administration. That is what gave her criticism weight. Relations with the United States are a cornerstone of European security. But a European leader who believes an American decision will help sustain Russia’s war economy ought to be able to say so in public. Meloni did.
Her letter to Costa brings the argument back to Europe. Individual leaders can hold talks with Putin, but who gave any one of them a mandate to speak for the other member states? Meloni wants the EU to agree on a representative at its December summit and to coordinate with Britain, Norway and other partners. Costa has agreed to raise the issue with EU leaders . By declining to put herself forward, Meloni has left her colleagues to answer the question on its merits. If they want Europe’s interests represented in negotiations, they must decide who has the authority to represent them.
In 2022, many judged Meloni by her party’s origins and her coalition partners’ ties to Moscow. Four years later, they can judge her by her decisions. She drew a line with Berlusconi when she needed his support to take office. She challenged Trump over a deal she believed would help finance Russia’s war. And she has told her own voters why defending Ukraine matters to Italy, even if some of them vote against her for it.
Those who casually dismissed Meloni as just another European populist owe the public an honest admission that they were wrong. As for her fellow European leaders, they might recall what she told Ukrainians in 2023. If Ukrainian freedom is the freedom of all Europe, surely it is worth risking an election for.
Dr. Orhan Dragaš is a Serbian expert on security and international relations. He is the founder and director of the International Security Institute, based in Belgrade; author of numerous expert articles, newspaper columns, as well as the books "The modern intelligence-security community, utopia or reality"; and; "Two faces of globalization – truth and deceptions."

articles.title_orig: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
articles.title_zh: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street

Oops, something went wrong
US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 4.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.5%, with the tech-heavy index closing in correction territory.
The Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) fell 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value.
The PHLX Semiconductor index ( ^SOX ) plummeted 12% as Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and other chip names sank. Wall Street unloaded this year's AI winners , while large-cap tech stocks saw the worst day since the COVID-19 pandemic sell-off.
Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy . Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill.
Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. Optimism grew overnight after Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost [the midterm elections] is the war," in a post on X suggesting the party should push for a resolution to the conflict. Brent crude oil ( BZ=F ) prices traded around $98 per barrel, while US benchmark WTI crude ( CL=F ) stood at $90 per barrel.
A report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023 as companies turned their attention to retaining existing employees, setting the scene for Friday's key employment report.
On the earnings calendar, Duke Energy ( DUK ), Airbnb ( ABNB ), and Lumentum ( LITE ), among others, report results.
Stocks plunged on Thursday amid carnage in the AI trade on Wall Street.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) plunged 4.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 5.5%, closing in correction territory.
Chip stocks took the brunt of the beating, with severe losses for Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ), among others. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank 12%.
Institutional investors dumped the top performers of 2026 to lock in gains. Retail traders followed suit, unloading $265 million of equities in their biggest selling day since 2020.
Meanwhile, regulatory concerns weighed on AI data center build-out stocks. SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) also plummeted over fears of regulatory hurdles following Democrats' congressional victory.
Retail investors are dumping US stocks at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $358 million in individual US stocks on Thursday as of 2:58 p.m. ET, according to Vanda Research, putting them on track for their biggest single-day net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
The selling marks a departure from retail investors' tendency to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued purchasing leveraged exchange-traded funds such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.
The AI trade's marquee stocks got clobbered on Thursday, sparking warnings on Wall Street of an institutional shakeout as investors move to lock in gains.
"They're shooting the generals," wrote Nomura cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott on Thursday.
The unwinding of the 2026 popular thematic stocks has been "wildly acute" for more than a month, the strategist noted. The primary catalyst isn't about a sudden deterioration in fundamentals, but a frantic dash by hedge funds to lock in their profits before the end of the year.
"Single-name stock moves are absolutely BONKERS," wrote McElligott. "The Momentum/High Sharpe unwind has been so substantial that we are approaching the dreaded 'Round Trip' levels in some trades."
The carnage has hit semiconductor and hardware stocks particularly hard. Shares of Lam Research ( LRCX ) are down 36% over the past month. Applied Materials ( AMAT ) has shed 30% over the past month, while AMD ( AMD ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are also down 22% and 15%, respectively, over the same period.
Goldman Sachs ( GS ) promoted 109 employees to its coveted partnership on Thursday, its largest class since 2010, as the Wall Street giant elevated record numbers of asset managers and engineers to its senior ranks.
The new class is nearly 15% larger than in 2024 when Goldman named 95 partners, according to a statement from the bank.
Of the 109 new partners, 60 work in Goldman's investment banking and trading division, while 33 are in Asset & Wealth Management. The firm also promoted 13 engineers.
In a departure from previous years, a Goldman executive declined to disclose the gender and racial makeup of the new class, citing changes in the legal environment. The executive added that with the latest round of promotions, the firm has more than 100 female partners.
Partnership status at Goldman is considered highly exclusive. The firm promotes new partners every two years. The promotion comes with higher compensation and additional financial benefits, including opportunities to invest in the firm's private funds.
Once promotions take effect in January, Goldman will have a little over 500 partners, an executive said, amounting to roughly 1% of Goldman's workforce.
It's a bad day for the stock market.
Major indexes are falling Thursday, with technology stocks leading the sell-off and semiconductor shares among the biggest decliners.
But one rough session doesn't necessarily amount to what investors deem a correction.
A correction generally refers to a decline of at least 10% from a recent high in a stock, index, or other asset. It is typically seen as a meaningful pullback, but one that stops short of a bear market, which is commonly defined as a drop of 20% or more.
That distinction matters after Wednesday's sharp rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) and the narrower Nasdaq-100 are each on pace to close Thursday in correction territory, as is the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ).
Meanwhile, the Dow and S&P 500 (down 3% and 4% from yesterday) aren't close to correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) just fell below its 200-day moving average, according to AlphaSpace data (see chart below).
Several individual names, such as Nvidia ( NVDA ), also broke through their 200-day averages, a technical indicator that tracks a stock's long-term trend.
"I think this has been brewing for quite some so much time because there have been so many investors poking at this perceived AI bubble, almost hoping it's going to burst, Hennion & Walsh chief investment officer Kevin Mahn told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
"So this type of volatility shouldn't necessarily come as a surprise to anybody … but there's going to be more choppiness ahead," Mahn added.
As AMD ( AMD ) stock falls 15% amid a chip stock rout on Thursday, the company's CEO Lisa Su told Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi she doesn't see the AI chips demand slowing down anytime soon.
"I think the market can sometimes be a little bit short-sighted. It is what it is," Su said on Sozzi Unleashed .
