articles.title_orig: An Update On A Possible ‘GTA 6’ PC Release Date Plans, Due To AI
articles.title_zh: An Update On A Possible ‘GTA 6’ PC Release Date Plans, Due To AI
articles.content_orig:
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU , we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.
The rise of AI-powered reverse-engineering tools —which can quickly turn a console game binary into easy-to-port raw code with incredible brute-force efficiency and minimal human effort—might change that kind of “PC can wait” calculus for Rockstar. “I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC,” Vermeij told Rock Paper Shotgun.
To be sure, decompiling a game as complex as Grand Theft Auto VI wouldn’t be as simple as, say, the previous human-led decompilations of early 3D GTA games . But even if an AI coding harness has some difficulty capturing all the details of GTA VI ‘s advanced weather systems and scripted sweat simulations , that doesn’t mean it’s impossible.
Vermeij speculated that reverse-engineering the console version of GTA VI could cost “tens of thousands of dollars in tokens,” and a resulting port probably “won’t be as good as [Rockstar’s] effort” in the end. That said, Vermeij said it would probably be good enough to satisfy some potential PC players and that he “wouldn’t be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together” to get ahead of that.
“What was the case before is that there’s so much effort in developing the game, that it is not possible to rip it off, and that’s completely changed now,” Vermeij said. “So, yeah, we’re going to have to see in the next couple of years how that’s going to pan out.”
While there hasn’t been an official timing announcement for the PC port of Grand Theft Auto VI , reports suggest Rockstar is currently aiming for the first quarter of 2027.

articles.title_orig: Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors
articles.title_zh: Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Investors are skeptical of many AI stocks right now, questioning the long-term return on investment for tech companies spending so much on data center infrastructure. And as a leading semiconductor company for AI infrastructure, Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has felt the pain from the sell-off, with its share price falling 13% over the past month.
That's put Nvidia's share price at around $202, far below analysts' average price target for Nvidia stock of $327. If it reaches that target, investors stand to gain around 62%. So, is now the right time to buy Nvidia stock, despite the concerns about AI spending?
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
I think so, especially given that recent tech earnings reports indicate tech companies are likely to continue investing in infrastructure over the next few years.
Let's start with SK Hynix 's (NASDAQ: SKHY) recently reported third-quarter results. The company is the leading high-bandwidth (HBM) memory company with 50% market share and the second-largest DRAM and NAND flash memory company with 24% and 19% market share, respectively.
The company has benefited immensely from a ramp-up in AI spending , sending its sales 328% higher in the quarter and its operating profit up 632%. Even more impressive is that the company's management said in a press release that 50% of its available memory supply for 2027-2028 is already sold out -- and that it expects its supply to remain constrained through 2030 .
What does this have to do with Nvidia? Well, SK Hynix is the leading supplier of HBM memory for many of Nvidia's data center components. If SK Hynix is experiencing exponential demand for its memory processors, part of that is due to Nvidia placing substantial orders. And if Nvidia is placing large orders for memory, it's because AI spending continues to rise.
This leads me to Alphabet' s and Microsoft 's recent cloud sales. These two companies hold a combined 35% of the cloud market, and they're both experiencing impressive sales gains from their AI spending. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled in the third quarter to $30.7 billion and Microsoft's Azure sales rose 48% to $33.2 billion.
Alphabet says it will spend up to $205 billion this year in capital expenditures (capex), mostly for AI. Microsoft says it will spend $170 billion in fiscal 2027. That's an acceleration of spending for both companies and it's a result of Microsoft and Alphabet realizing that their cloud investments are paying off.
And they're not the only ones. Bank of America said recently that AI data center spending is estimated to more than double to $2.1 trillion by 2028. While investors are rightly concerned that some AI spending is too high and won't be worth the investment, Alphabet and Microsoft are already benefiting from their spending and are doubling down.
Again, that's great news for Nvidia because these two companies are critical customers for Nvidia, and it's a good indicator that AI infrastructure investments aren't slowing down yet.
Nvidia's shares have a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 26 right now, which makes them slightly cheaper than the tech sector P/E average of 28.5. Investors don't have to back the truck up and go all-in on Nvidia stock right now. But the recent pullback does present a buying opportunity for some investors to start a small position or add to an existing one.
The chipmaker will report its fiscal 2027's third quarter results on Nov. 17 and Wall Street's consensus estimates are for earnings per share of $2.47 and nearly $109 billion in sales. Considering Nvidia has beaten analysts' earnings estimates in seven of the past eight quarters, shareholders could be pleasantly surprised again soon.
More importantly, with Nvidia's customers already experiencing significant growth and continuing to invest in AI, Nvidia's long-term growth prospects remain intact.

articles.title_orig: 31-year-old dumpster diver brought in $140,000 in 12 months: I 'did much more than I thought was possible'
articles.title_zh: 31-year-old dumpster diver brought in $140,000 in 12 months: I 'did much more than I thought was possible'
articles.content_orig:
When Carter Stevens tells people he makes six figures a year digging through dumpsters, they often assume he's "blowing smoke," he says.
Not everyone sees dollar signs in a brimming dumpster. But Stevens earned roughly $140,000 in total sales between September 2025 and September 2026 by salvaging trashed items, cleaning them up and selling them on platforms like eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It.
Stevens primarily operates near office parks and luxury condominiums around Nashville, Tennessee. Since March 2024, when he started dumpster diving, he's found and sold hand-crafted Persian rugs, high-end office chairs and even samurai swords, he says. Trash-picking helps him keep his shipping costs low, he adds: Some of his supplies, like cardboard boxes and packing tape, also come from dumpsters, enough that he doesn't have to pay for them approximately "90% of the time."
"The amount of waste in this country that you'll find is unbelievable. We throw so much stuff out," says Stevens, 31.
Sometimes, Stevens asks a building for permission to go through its trash, marketing himself as a junk removal service. In that way, his job is similar — though not identical, because he generally only takes what he can sell, he says — to other entrepreneurs across the U.S. who follow advice in Reddit threads or YouTube tutorials to launch junk removal side hustles or full-time businesses . There are around 10,000 junk removal businesses across the U.S., according to the Better Business Bureau. They range in scale from independent side hustles to national companies like 1-800-GOT-JUNK , which touts more than 150 franchise locations.
Other times, Stevens finds himself neck deep in rubbish, ducking concerned security guards, peeling away actual trash and rotting food in the hope of uncovering discarded treasure, he says. He tries to avoid sneaking around and keeps an eye out for "no trespassing" signs. He'd rather leave items behind if a property owner or security guard tells him to vacate the premises, he says.
Even Stevens expresses surprise at how much money he's made, saying he doesn't necessarily think his annual income is sustainable. When he "stumbled into" dumpster diving, he was approximately $12,000 in debt after years of poor spending habits fueled partially by a drug addiction, a stark change from his affluent childhood, he says.
"I dug myself out of a hole. I built up my savings. I really did much more than I thought was possible," says Stevens.
Stevens, a Nashville native, is the son of a five-time Grammy Award-winning producer of country and gospel music who has worked with artists like Blake Shelton and Carrie Underwood. His life took a turn in college when he developed an addiction to prescription Adderall, leading him to drop out partway through his senior year in 2018, he says.
His lack of a college degree made landing full-time work a challenge. He says his parents can afford to support him financially, and they've done so in specific emergency occasions. But mostly, his father wants his kids to learn to fend for themselves, he says: "He will let me sit on the coals for the sake of learning how to swim. That's taught me a lot [and] given me a lot of valuable skills and a tough mentality."
Unemployed, Stevens started combing through thrift shops and Goodwill clothing racks for vintage apparel to sell on eBay. He was inspired by YouTube influencers like Rick Senko, he says, whose Fort Lauderdale, Florida-based clothing resale business Technsports brought in $6.5 million in annual revenue as recently as 2024.
But Stevens' returns were inconsistent, and he often spent his profits on drugs or luxury shopping sprees, he says. After his parents funded a rehab stint in 2021 — helping him "quit doing the hard drugs," he says — he spent his money chasing other dopamine hits. Those indulgences included a $1,200 pair of Christian Dior Birkenstock sandals, an 85-inch flat-screen television and a $30,000 down payment on a Mercedes-AMG sedan that he later lost because he couldn't afford the total cost, he says.
By June 2023, he could no longer afford to pay rent, so he lived in a rented storage unit until the business's security found and evicted him, and then stayed in his Nissan Sentra for three weeks, he says. Homelessness shocked him into learning to manage his "reckless" spending habits, he says: "Being punished by your own spending addiction was a wringer that I promised myself I can't be put through again."
In October 2023, a cousin lent him money to start renting an apartment, and Stevens worked to stick to a sensible enough budget for his thrifting income to cover future rent and basic expenses, he says. Five months later, he found a discarded pair of black Nike Air Force Ones in good condition next to a gas station pump. He took them home, sanitized them and sold them online for $35, he says.
"That was the first time I had ever found something that was trash and sold it and made a little bit of money," says Stevens.
Once he started dumpster diving, Stevens was hooked "because I never stopped finding good stuff in these dumpsters," he says.
His biggest score to date: dozens of discarded Steelcase office chairs, worth $1,000-plus each when new, outside an overflowing office park dumpster, he says. He got his car — by this point, a used pickup truck and a self-built trailer — and hauled away 190 chairs to list online at hundreds of dollars apiece. He sold the majority of them in bulk transactions on Facebook Marketplace for $17,000, and brought in an additional $10,600 selling the remaining chairs individually, documents show.
If Stevens manages to find roughly one valuable haul per month, he can fill his $400-a-month storage unit and start listing the items. For the most part, he scopes out corporate environments, preferring "dry dumpsters" over ones laden with food waste, he says. Office trash is particularly profitable when companies downsize, says Stevens: Once, he found 120 standing desks discarded outside a building.
Near high-end apartment buildings, Stevens has found furniture from brands like West Elm, iPads, electronics and power tools in working condition, he says. "Almost every piece of furniture in my apartment came from a dumpster," says Stevens.
Stevens works alone and minimizes gas costs by sticking to locations within a few miles from his apartment. The majority of his income has come from big hauls across his five highest-earning months, reflecting the venture's hit-or-miss nature. "I got really lucky earlier this year and I made a ton of money. I'm not acting like this is something I could do every year," he says.
So he saves as much of his earnings as possible, "constantly" talking himself out of unnecessary purchases, he says. And he's studying the business of real estate wholesaling — which involves securing contracts for distressed properties and flipping them to investors for a fee — as a potentially more secure way to earn a living, he adds.
Still, he acknowledges the allure of knowing his next big payday could always be one dumpster away.
"I don't see myself ever turning down a good looking dumpster," says Stevens. "I have found so much cool stuff that I feel like I'll always be curious about what's in that dumpster."

articles.title_orig: BioWare Lives On: Here Are All The Post-BioWare Projects Currently In Production
articles.title_zh: BioWare Lives On: Here Are All The Post-BioWare Projects Currently In Production
articles.content_orig:
International TV Co-Editor
EXCLUSIVE: The final days of legendary video games studio BioWare will be told in a doc from Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie for Canada ‘s Super Channel .
Massive Effect: The BioWare Story will document how the Edmonton, Canada-based games company grew from being founded in 1995 by three medical doctors – Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip – to selling 100 million copies of its role-playing games, which include Mass Effect , Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic , Dragon Age and Baldur’s Gate .
Written and directed by Akash Sherman ( Clara ) and co-produced by Canada’s Fennessey Films and Score G Productions , the film has a unique insight into the story, with filming beginning two years before Electronic Arts announced the closure of BioWare on October 21 last month and continuing to lens throughout.
This allowed the filmmakers to capture BioWare’s finale chapter, as the news of the studio’s closure reverberated through the gaming industry. EA decided to shutter studio, which was known for its complex narratives and world building, after recent releases underperformed, and 400 jobs were cut.
Muzyka, Zeschuk and Yip will feature in the film, along with a plethora of major players from the video game world. These include Douglas Reilly, Vice President of Lucasfilm Games; John Riccitiello, former CEO of Electronic Arts; Casey Hudson, game director of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect ; Geoff Keighley, creator of The Game Awards; Victor Lucas, creator of The Electric Playground ; voice actor Jennifer Hale; and longtime BioWare developers Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone.
“When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and genuinely moved,” said BioWare co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk in a statement.
“BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about deeply emotionally engaging stories and characters, brought to life by the amazingly talented people on our dev teams, and our excellent production and distribution partners who helped us bring those stories successfully to all corners of the planet, and our passionate fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again.”
A website has also been set up for the BioWare community to share photos, videos and how the company touched their lives for the chance to appear in the film. “BioWare’s fans have been part of its journey since the very first game,” said Scorgie. “It’s only right that they help us tell the rest of the story.”
“The BioWare founders are my hometown heroes,” added writer and director Sherman. “It’s a privilege and responsibility to share the journey of underdogs who came together to create deeply beloved storytelling. Their golden era kindled a spark in me and in an entire generation. With the studio’s recent closure, the film is now a profound valediction.”
Canada’s Super Channel commissioned the doc, which is being planned for a major film festival run and a world premiere next year. Jhod Cardinal of Upstream Flix is handling worldwide sales. The Canada Media Fund supported production.
“We are thrilled to bring Massive Effect: The BioWare Story to Canadian audiences,” said Kim Ball, EVP Content & Communications for Super Channel. “As an Edmonton-based company, we’re especially proud to celebrate BioWare’s extraordinary hometown story and the people, creativity and groundbreaking storytelling behind some of the most beloved games of a generation.”
Producers Fennessey Films and Score G are behind the likes of Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story , Dolph: Unbreakable , Inmate #1: The Rise of Danny Trejo , Breaking Olympia , Singhs in the Ring and The Great Ones .

articles.title_orig: Boeing retirees are hit with 400% increase in Medicare Advantage premiums
articles.title_zh: Boeing retirees are hit with 400% increase in Medicare Advantage premiums
articles.content_orig:
Christopher McMahon is thinking about going back to work.
The 65-year-old retired from Boeing in 2022 after over three decades in the company’s Seattle-area offices. But the spiking cost of health insurance has him considering whether to get a part-time job.
McMahon, who lives in Des Moines, is enrolled in an Aetna Medicare Advantage plan sponsored by Boeing for its retirees. He and his wife currently pay premiums totaling around $120 per month. Next year, those premiums will jump to over $630 per month for the couple.
That’s an increase of more than 400%.
“We’re shocked,” he said. “This is just so much more than we thought it would be. This is just awful.”
When people turn 65, they become eligible for Medicare, the public insurance program for older adults. At that point, they can choose to enroll in Medicare Advantage, a private insurance option that’s typically more affordable than traditional Medicare, though it comes with restrictions like prior authorization requirements and limited doctor networks.
Some employers offer group Medicare Advantage plans to workers as a retirement benefit. But retirees of Boeing — one of the biggest employers in Washington — are questioning whether they can afford the benefit that was once practically free.
When Boeing first introduced its Aetna Medicare Advantage plan in 2024, the coverage came with a $0 premium, and it remained $0 through 2025.
At the start of this year, Aetna began charging a $60 monthly premium per enrollee. Next year, monthly premiums will have a dramatic increase to $316 per enrollee. The company doesn’t pay for premiums, meaning retirees have to shoulder the increase on their own.
Before 2024, Boeing offered retirees a Medicare Supplement plan, which is a different type of coverage. According to the company, that plan cost enrollees between $327 and $370 per month.
“To me it’s just outrageous,” said Gayle Hughes, who retired from Boeing in 2020 after working at the company for 33 years.
Boeing retirees don’t have to buy coverage through the company, and there are many Medicare Advantage plans available to people in  Washington with premiums as low as $0 per month, though lower-priced plans come with more restrictions.
But Hughes is reluctant to switch plans, because she doesn’t want to lose access to Aetna’s network of doctors. People who drop Boeing’s plan cannot sign back up in the future.
Hughes and her husband plan to stay on the plan for one more year, with the hope that premiums will come back down afterward.
The premium increases come at a shaky time for the Medicare Advantage market. Over the past few years, insurance companies have shrunk their provider networks, raised out-of-pocket costs and eliminated plans that fail to make money. Health insurance premiums in general are rising rapidly , driven by high medical spending and inflation.
In an email, a Boeing spokesperson attributed next year’s higher premiums to rising healthcare claims and plan costs. Aetna did not respond to a request for comment.
Without any help, retirees are struggling to figure out how to absorb the higher costs.
Gordon Hale enrolled in Boeing’s Medicare Advantage plan in September when he turned 65. The upcoming increase will translate to an extra $3,000 in premiums over the course of a year for just himself. To afford it, he foresees some belt-tightening.
He expects that he’ll have to delay some maintenance on his house, including a roof replacement. Hale had planned to take his daughter on a trip during her spring break next year. “That’s probably a staycation now,” he said.
Medicare Advantage premiums are not the only cost of health insurance for older adults.
Most people over 65 also have to pay a standard premium known as the Part B premium, which is adjusted based on income; many have to pay a separate, income-based premium for drug coverage, too.
For some, the combined cost of premiums have spurred a realization that retirement might be more expensive than they anticipated.
Next year, McMahon, of Des Moines, estimates that he and his wife will have to spend at least $2,000 per month on health coverage, after combining all their premium costs and income-based adjustments.
For extra money, the couple have decided to start withdrawing Social Security payments earlier than they had planned. They’ll be hit with a penalty for doing so. They’re also considering dropping the Boeing Medicare Advantage plan for something cheaper, though it might not come with the same level of coverage.
Most likely, McMahon expects that he’ll have to go back to work in some capacity.
“I’m really terrified that we’re going to run out of money,” he said.
It’s not what he wants. McMahon has been enjoying retirement. He likes to wake up early, make his wife a latte and tackle a different project every day, like doing repairs in his garage or pruning back the roses in his garden.
“I’m not at all bored,” he said. “I really have no interest in going back to work.” But he might not have a choice.
He heard about a new retirement housing facility opening up in Des Moines. He’s considering applying for a job there.

articles.title_orig: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.title_zh: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Sen. Chris Coons, next chair of key committees on foreign policy and defense, sees a path despite the president’s veto power.
U .S. Sen. Chris Coons’ phone has been blowing up nonstop ever since the Election Day blue tsunami . Bing, bing, bing go the incoming text messages.
No wonder. On Jan. 3, the Delaware Democrat will become chairman of both the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the Senate subcommittee that allocates funds for the military and national security agencies.
Foreign capitals are anxious to decipher how the U.S. public’s rebuff of President Donald Trump will affect his foreign policy, especially on tariffs and the Iran war. “I think my count is 27 ambassadors, two foreign ministers, and one head of state in the last 48 hours,” Coons said.
American voters, even those who don’t ordinarily focus on foreign policy, told pollsters they (rightly) blame Trump’s incoherent Iran war and his tariffs for the rise in fuel and food prices. They are linking affordability to foreign policy and expect the Democrats to change course.
I asked the senator whether a Democratic-controlled Congress had the tools to revamp the president’s destructive foreign policy. His response was quick: “Congress always has the power of the purse.” His caveats came later.
As we spoke, Coons laid out a scenario about how that power, wielded by Democrats and disgruntled Republicans , might be brought to bear in the upcoming lame-duck session of Congress, even before the Democrats take charge next year.
This gets a bit complicated, but please read on.
By Dec. 11, the Senate must authorize overall spending for military and security programs for fiscal year 2027, which includes the Pentagon. The White House is also seeking a supplemental $350 billion for defense , over which Congress would have no future say.
“There are a number of Republican senators who are deeply unhappy about Trump for ending their careers, who support Ukraine and question the war with Iran, and now you’ve had a stinging rebuke of the Republican Party,” Coons told me. “So why would they vote for the $350 billion and not fight for funding for Ukraine and for a change in direction on the war with Iran?”
» READ MORE: U.S. oligarchs who act at Trump’s behest do so at their peril | Trudy Rubin
Thanks to those GOP senators — a group that includes John Cornyn, Thom Tillis, Bill Cassidy, Mitch McConnell, and others — Coons does not think this supplemental will be passed this year.
As for Ukraine, he believes there will be much stronger support when Democrats take over, and perhaps even in this session, for releasing limited funds already appropriated for Kyiv before Trump cut off all funding. The senator would also like to hold hearings on who was responsible for recently degrading vital Starlink services to Ukraine.
“It should be our priority that we help Ukraine get through the winter both by more actively coordinating the transfer of PAC3 Patriot missiles and authorizing transfer of technology to NATO partners to manufacture more of them,” Coons said.
So far, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has refused to release a tranche of missiles to Ukraine already paid for by European governments.
“We should say to the Europeans, ‘If you are willing to buy [the missiles], we are willing to sell them,’” he said.
So can Democrats influence foreign policy before the end of the year? “Yes, in partnership with disaffected and retiring Republicans,” Coons said. Can Democrats influence foreign policy next year? “Likely yes, through the defense authorization bill,” he added.
Coons emphasized that Trump wouldn’t be able to get any ambassadors or senior policy people or judges confirmed “without working with us.”
The senator also stressed that voters have clearly connected tariffs and the Iran war with the rising cost of living. GOP senators who are running for reelection in two years may not wish to be associated with support for either, even if Trump still backs both.
As for whether the president might launch another major attack on Iran this year, Coons offered, “My hunch is that you will pretty quickly see enough Republicans abandoning support for the war to give Trump the opportunity to say, ‘I am not going to launch a renewed war in partnership with [Benjamin] Netanyahu.’” Of course, Israel’s recent inconclusive elections, which may not produce a new government for weeks , also figure in the calculations.
Another wild card is that departing Kentucky GOP congressman and Trump antagonist, Thomas Massie, has pledged to force a vote this week on impeaching Hegseth. Coons believes there are so many resentful Republicans that Massie could succeed.
Although he doesn’t think impeachment is a good use of the new majority’s time in 2027 (and wouldn’t succeed with Trump, anyway), he believes that Hegseth’s case is different. “It’s focused on one of the main drivers of the costs that voters are upset about,” he explained.
» READ MORE: The Israeli opposition can still defeat Netanyahu — if it will accept the support of Israeli Arab political parties | Trudy Rubin
An impeachment process would also inform the public of how deeply Hegseth has undercut the American military and weakened U.S. security abroad.
And the hearings Coons intends to hold — including on the tightening links between Trump favorites Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Kim Jong Un and their aid to Iran — may finally break through the public’s blindness about Trump’s love of dictators who wish America ill.
The senator also wants to examine the dangers to America posed by the gutting of the U.S. Department of State and international development aid. Yet, Coons is not naive about the powers Trump retains, nor his threat to become “Mr. Veto” and sink bills Democrats get passed.
Coons noted that he was “in an optimistic mood because my party just had the biggest night in my adult life. It is entirely possible that Trump’s id will not allow him to accept his loss, and he’ll use his powers to overthrow the government in Cuba, return to bombing Iran, and continue threatening the Canadians and the Europeans.
“I mean, of course he could. I mean, he’s Trump.”
Yup. But given the incredible events on Election Day, I prefer to put aside skepticism and focus on the new opportunities the Delaware senator laid out.
After Tuesday, there are possibilities for change that may begin to rescue American foreign policy from the nightmare of the last two years.

It is hatred of Jews with a new label. Replacing the word “Jewish” with “Zionist” does not change who is being targeted, writes Andrew Goretsky.
For all of the talk about threats to democracy, the key issues for many voters were economic, not constitutional. That raises the question of what Americans would have tolerated if prices were better.
Plus: Policy advice for Democrats as they enjoy their trifecta, and simpler solutions for building more housing in Philadelphia.

The Democrat’s record of constructive accomplishment was rewarded by voters Tuesday, offering a dramatic contrast with their rejection of President Trump.
There were no seized ballots, no troops at the polls — and a record turnout. America was never cut out for dictatorship.
There is a difference between legitimate oversight and deciding in advance that impeachment will define the next Congress.

articles.title_orig: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.title_zh: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.content_orig:
Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.
The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.
From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.
Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases .
More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.
"People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public."
Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman . But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.
"Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more."
Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.
Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.
"I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public."
Anthropic declined to comment.
AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers  simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion , "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.
In the risk factors section of its prospectus , Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.
Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.
"There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny."
Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over."
Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.
The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development.
"Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good."

articles.title_orig: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
articles.title_zh: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
articles.content_orig:
Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient
I t was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.
Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers . Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.
But freezers present a new vulnerability. In Sweden, for example, some of the stores that were attacked this week hadn’t connected their freezers to national retailers’ systems, which have centralised protection. Now they’ve learned their lesson the hard way.
Hybrid warfare – or, to use the defence term, greyzone aggression – refers to an array of hostile acts by a country’s adversaries that fall short of full-on military conflict. Cyber-hackers also this week attempted to meddle with fridges at French blood banks, while hoax bomb threats forced commercial airliners across Europe to divert, make emergency landings or require fighter jet escort to safety.
This comes after at least two years of sporadic Kremlin-suspected arson attacks on factories, explosives-laden drones flown into airports and drone incursions into countries’ airspace. There is constant GPS interference in the skies around the Baltic Sea, highly suspicious damage to subsea cables and pipelines, disinformation spread by bot farms and repeated acts of cyber-aggression.
Saboteurs and hackers usually have two aims: the first is to disrupt, but they also want to psychologically destabilise the target societies by spreading fear. It is fortunate then that the aviation hoaxes and freezer incidents coincide with a renewed conversation across Europe about resilience. It is as if the hackers wanted to showcase the need for preparedness projects such as the UK government’s new Be Ready campaign , which launched last month.
The British campaign, which instructs people on such things as stockpiling for emergencies whether caused by climate change or state-sponsored terrorism, had been in the works for months. Ministers hesitated however, fearing that citizens would respond with cynicism or ridicule, or just wouldn’t follow the advice.
Such campaigns are commonplace elsewhere. Earthquake zones such as Tokyo and San Francisco have had them for decades. “Make a Plan. Gather Supplies. Get Connected. Get Trained,” are the San Francisco city government’s pillars of instruction .
The newest version of Sweden’s official booklet In Case of Crisis or War , distributed to every home since 2018, is even more comprehensive, with clear language about everything from civil defence duties, how to volunteer (give blood or team up with neighbours for mutual support), to what items always to have at home, and how to find out if a crisis is real or a fake warning by bots.
For several years, I have been calling on the UK to follow Sweden’s lead and send a similar instruction leaflet to UK households, only to be told by officials that doing so would cause too much panic and frighten people. A House of Lords committee heard from the chair of the UK National Preparedness Commission in March that “the bulk of the UK population is blissfully unaware” of some of the risks they face.
It turns out that British people are less cynical than their leaders had assumed. Perhaps a few minds were also changed by Covid-19, which dramatically illustrated how vulnerable globalised and open societies are to all manner of threats.
after newsletter promotion
Either way, within a week of the Be Ready campaign launching, the retailer Robert Dyas reported that weekly sales of radios had shot up by 160%. Maplin reported that sales of radios had nearly doubled and sales of power banks had more than doubled, while torch sales had soared to nearly four times the usual figure.
The puddles of defrosted ice in the supermarket aisles and stress for air travellers this week show that we need to be prepared for a very wide range of threats including power and water outages. We have already seen what happens to our complex food supply chains when global shipping lanes are suddenly disrupted. Iran’s obstruction of the strait of Hormuz following US airstrikes has given us painful food inflation and costly global oil and fertiliser shortages.
But what if the ships importing the food we eat can no longer make it to our ports? No industrialised nation grows all the food it consumes. What if the internet goes down? It’s not impossible. Even companies with the best cyber defence could fall victim to sabotage of the subsea data cables that transmit nearly all our connectivity.
This week has been a nasty preview of what could happen in future with alarming regularity. Severe disruption will come our way so simply hoping for the best is not an option. The good news is that by accepting that we need to prepare, and demonstrating that we remain strong in times of crisis, we can signal to Vladimir Putin and other rogue actors that disrupting our services is unwelcome, but ultimately it is futile.
Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War : The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.title_zh: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off .
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire more than doubled its share repurchases last quarter to $9.6 billion, while operating earnings declined slightly, the company said on Saturday .
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite , which fell 3.4% on the week.
Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a " correction ," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday .
Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a " significant opportunity " ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.
He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet , saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and " we saw Google as a significant player . "
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.
As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.
It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett .
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion , falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)
Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"
But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's , however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses ," Chevron , and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon , HP , Paramount (now Skydance) , General Motors , Constellation Brands , and Pool .
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.
Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion . The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.
A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.
This week, Reuters reports , Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."

articles.title_zh: Dozens killed as humanitarian crisis mounts in Yemen: What next for war?
articles.content_orig:
Airstrikes in a town near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, have killed 22 people and wounded 30 others, mostly women and children, according to a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry
CAIRO -- Airstrikes in a town near the capital, Sanaa, on Saturday killed 22 people and wounded 30 others, mostly women and children, a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said.
Speaking to The Associated Press, Anees Alasbahi accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the strikes in the village of al-Shariya. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The attacks came a day after Houthi officials said 30 people were killed in strikes on a market in southern Yemen. The Iranian-backed Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed military each blamed the other for that strike.

articles.title_orig: Governor-Elect of Texas Announces Plans to Bring Elon Musk Under Control
articles.title_zh: Governor-Elect of Texas Announces Plans to Bring Elon Musk Under Control
articles.content_orig:
The governor-elect of Texas Gina Hinojosa made it clear on the campaign trail that she would work to rein in data centers and billionaire tech barons. And now that she’s headed into office, that means playing hardball with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
“We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms,” Hinojosa said Thursday in an interview with CNN , as quoted by Bloomberg . “It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”
A central part of Hinojosa’s campaign was demanding an immediate moratorium on new data center construction until lawmakers have established tighter regulations and stronger protections for local communities.
In the Thursday interview, Hinojosa reiterated her commitment to placing more stringent regulations on data centers by saying she would “balance” it with keeping Texas a business-friendly state.
She also shared that she’s already making moves to crack down on Musk. Amid speculation that Texas officials have been considering a sale of state park land to SpaceX, Hinojosa said she spoke to the head of the Texas Parks & Wildlife Department to “request that no action be taken,” per Bloomberg .
“It is such an important resource,” she told reporters in Austin, hours before the CNN interview.
Wall Street and the AI industry are watching Hinojosa closely, as Texas has become the nucleus of the data center boom. Over a quarter of the US’s planned data center capacity resides in the state.
Musk is deeply invested in the state, having relocated his companies SpaceX and Tesla there from California. He’s also reportedly exploring sites to build another large data center in Texas , to add to the controversial “Colossus” facilities he operates in Greater Memphis. That’s not to mention the quarter of a billion dollars he poured into the midterms to support Republican candidates.
Of course, Musk could simply do what many think is impossible — or at least economically infeasible — and ditch terrestrial AI instrastructure altogether.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X , following the brutal election loss.

articles.title_orig: How Chicago businesses are bracing for the state's hemp ban
articles.title_zh: How Chicago businesses are bracing for the state's hemp ban
articles.content_orig:
Why are we asking for donations?
A display of THC beverages at the Humboldt Park offices of Perfectly Dosed. The company makes THC emulsion ingredients for a number of companies, including about 50 Illinois businesses.
Provided by South Loop Market
Marz Community Brewing Co. recovered from the post-pandemic downturn with the help of hemp-derived THC beverages.
Their infused line, which includes low-dose and high-potency THC seltzers with playful names like Bong Water and High Tea, has grown to account for nearly half the company’s production at its headquarters in McKinley Park and its Logan Square nanobrewery and taproom.
“It truly rescued our business and allowed us to expand,” Marz founder Ed Marszewski said.
Ed Marszewski, owner of Marz Brewing, stands in front of a fridge of a collection of non-alcoholic drinks at Life on Marz at 1950 N. Western, Wednesday, Nov. 26, 2025. | Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Strong local demand for THC drinks even pushed the company to relocate some of its beer production to Louisville, Kentucky, where its partner Against the Grain Brewery has co-packed and brewed several Marz beers the last few years.
But with the state’s looming Nov. 12 deadline banning nearly every intoxicating hemp product on the market, Marszewski and many other Chicago businesses must make some tough decisions.
“We’re going to have to lay people off,” Marszewski said. “We won’t have enough income to pay them.”
The ban is part a wide-ranging bill, signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in June , that overhauls cannabis and hemp regulations. But the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association and a group of hemp businesses filed an emergency motion on Friday for a temporary restraining order saying the law is unconstitutional and would “obliterate the businesses of thousands of Illinois farmers, infusers, distributors, and retailers.”
The state’s timetable mimicked federal guidelines set in President Donald Trump’s 2025 spending bill that also outlawed hemp potency limits beyond 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Previously, hemp-based THC products were federally defined as having less than 0.3% THC, the active ingredient in cannabis.
In September, the federal deadline was extended to Dec. 11, but Illinois has stuck with the original November deadline — keeping the pressure on beverage manufacturers, retailers, restaurants, grocery stores, entertainment venues and other stakeholders.
With Illinois businesses required to exit the category a month ahead of other states, local breweries are at a particular disadvantage against neighboring competitors, according to Jonathan Fritz, partner at Hopewell Brewing Co., which launched its popular lemon-lime-flavored THC drink Choom in 2024 before expanding to sparkling waters and teas.
Hopewell Brewing Co. launched its popular lemon-lime-flavored THC drink Choom in 2024 but will be winding down the product following new regulations for hemp-based THC products.
As part of an inventory wind down, the company is offering 50% off Choom products at its Logan Square headquarters, where it also co-manufactures THC beverages for other brands.
“Our state legislators have missed the mark here, and this decision directly damages local craft businesses like ours,” Fritz said.
Hopewell’s THC line has been carried at Parson’s Chicken & Fish, Foxtrot and other stores, accounting for nearly a third of its on-premises sales, the company told the Sun-Times last year.
Revolution Brewing, Chicago’s largest independent craft brewer, halted production of its Reverb THC beverage line in the summer.
Revolution owner Josh Deth hopes Congress can find a resolution and that Illinois lawmakers follow suit by allowing distribution through licensed liquor establishments, a carve-out strongly favored by alcohol suppliers, distributors and retailers.
“There’s clear customer demand for low-dosage THC beverages for both drinking at home and going out, and we’d love to keep innovating within the THC drink space if we are allowed too,” he said.
London-based research firm Euromonitor International estimated the hemp-based THC beverage market will skyrocket to $4.1 billion by 2028, an eye-popping 1,615% increase from $239 million in 2023.
Humboldt Park-based Perfectly Dosed makes THC emulsion ingredients for about 50 Illinois beverage brands, breweries and restaurants. It’s planning to move some warehousing and fulfillment services out of state if restrictions are prolonged.
Several of its partners and suppliers extract hemp in Colorado, which has emerged as a potential build-out site due its safe harbor laws.
“We do have to consider that as an option,” Perfectly Dosed co-founder Glenn McElfresh said. “The question that a lot of businesses are facing, including ourselves right now, is where do we invest that future CapEx [capital expenditure] for our business?”
Perfectly Dosed Vice President of Government Affairs Glenn McElfresh, CEO Alexander Choi and Vice President of Business Development Liam Rigney at the company’s headquarters in Humboldt Park. The co-founders plan to move some warehousing and fulfillment services out of state if Illinois’ hemp restrictions are enacted and prolonged.
Barry Brecheisen/For the Sun-Times
His assessment of the Illinois market has changed drastically since about a year ago when he told the Sun-Times that Chicago could become the heart of the hemp beverage industry.
“Because of the law, we can’t definitely say we’re going to build in Illinois,” McElfresh said.
Perfectly Dosed plans to apply for a newly established hemp product manufacturing license administered through the Illinois Department of Agriculture.
Licenses will be required for any business or person handling, processing and extracting hemp in Illinois, as well as manufacturing any product with hemp-extracted cannabinoids or any hemp-derived product, according to the Illinois Department of Agriculture.
Manufacturing licenses will be issued after applications and on-site inspections are completed and a $5,000 fee is paid.
The department didn’t share how many businesses have already applied for a license but said in a statement that it’s working with “several applicants as they complete the process.” It also said that it’s “accepting applications for both hemp manufacturing and industrial hemp processor licenses on a rolling basis, with no application deadline.”
Cresco Labs CEO Charlie Bachtell said it supports regulatory standards for all THC products. The Chicago-based vertically integrated company operates 10 stores in Illinois, including two in Chicago.
“Consumers deserve to know what they’re buying and that they can rely on production and testing standards for products they ingest,” he said.
A sign warning of an impending ban on some THC beverages stands outside of a BP gas station at 1221 S. Wabash Ave. on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.
Tim O’Hern, chief operating officer of Nature’s Grace and Wellness in Fulton County, expects several products sold outside licensed cannabis channels to transition into the regulated market.
“THC beverages represent one of the fastest growing product categories in the regulated cannabis industry,” O’Hern said. Nature’s Grace operates nine stores in Illinois, including three in Chicago.
Cannabis product sales in Ohio’s regulated market increased significantly since the state implemented a hemp products ban in March, benefiting companies like Chicago-based Verano Holdings, which operates six stores in the state.
“According to state data, total receipts were up 25% at the end of the third quarter versus the end of the first quarter, a notable positive trend that correlates with the start of the hemp ban, which indicates hemp consumers are shifting towards licensed dispensaries,” Verano Holdings founder and CEO George Archos told analysts last month.
Under Illinois’ new guidelines, hemp-derived THC products over the federal potency threshold must be sold only at state-licensed cannabis dispensaries and be taxed the same as cannabis products

articles.title_zh: Palestinian citizens of Israel put to ‘loyalty test’ after election wins
articles.content_orig:
Tel Aviv-Jaffa, Israel – On election day, Lama Yassin, 31, drove to polling stations in her hometown of Arrabeh, where Palestinian citizens of Israel make up an overwhelming majority, inspired by what she was witnessing.
“You would see families coming to the polls together, grandparents and grandchildren,” she said. “It was the first time in a really long time that I felt there is hope – hope of a change.”
The overwhelming Arab turnout in the October 27 Israeli election won the Arab parties a record 19 seats in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament.
Thabet Abu Rass, an expert on Jewish-Arab relations in Israel, had predicted the Arab parties would be impossible for Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc to ignore: Their seats push it past the 61-seat threshold for a ruling coalition.
Instead, Yassin and others saw Israeli channels invite “Jews to talk about Arabs and Arab voter turnout”, she recalled, with almost no Arab guests.
“The whole conversation was about how dangerous these Arab voters are.” The “most disgusting term” she saw online, however, was the repeated refrain of “election terrorism” on Channel 14, the hard-right, pro-Netanyahu station.
Within a day of the vote, Likud and figures like Itamar Ben-Gvir accused the Arab parties of stealing the election through “bribery, threats, violence, forgeries”. The accusations have continued even after the Central Elections Committee and the Israeli police said they found no sign of organised tampering.
Distraught, Yassin posted an Instagram video that went viral among Palestinians, capturing the doublespeak of Israelis they so often hear:
“Eating hummus with us? ‘Brothers and friends’.
Seeking political power? ‘Terror supporters’.
Helping someone in distress? ‘Brothers and friends’.
Voting in large numbers? ‘Terror at the ballot box’.”
“When it suits you, we are brothers and friends. When it suits you, we are a symbol of coexistence. When it suits you, you go around the world boasting about our integration into Israeli society.
“But the moment we demand to have influence, to shape policy, and to take part in decision-making – suddenly, our very presence becomes a threat.”
More than a week after the election, Jaffa’s Ajami neighbourhood offers both the history leading up to – and the fraught circumstances of – this moment that Abu Rass calls Israel’s “political crossroads”.
Faded Arabic signs on abandoned buildings hint at the Palestinian community that thrived in Ajami before 1948. On Ajami’s streets, posters of children killed during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza hang metres away from campaign posters for Ra’am and the Joint List.
From the back office of his cluttered hardware shop, Omar Siksik, once a Tel Aviv-Jaffa city councilman who now co-chairs Kulna Yaffa, a grassroots, Arab-Jewish civic initiative in the city, weighs this moment of unprecedented representation – met by renewed delegitimisation efforts – against Ajami’s own history. It is a struggle, he says, for basic existence.
Before 1948, Jaffa had about 100,000 Palestinians. After the Nakba, fewer than 4,000 remained – with those left fenced inside Ajami under military rule. “We called it the Ajami ghetto,” explained Siksik. Born there in 1957, he grew up sharing a toilet and kitchen with newly arrived Jewish immigrants who took the homes of expelled Palestinian neighbours.
Over time, the fence surrounding Ajami was torn down, martial law ended, and the Palestinians who remained there were granted Israeli citizenship. But later, when Siksik became the head of the Rabita Association, a nonprofit for the Palestinian residents of Jaffa, he remembered “sleeping under the bulldozers” that were razing the houses of Palestinians in the area, a practice that Rabita had fought in court.
For Siksik and others, election day is the only occasion that’s different for Palestinian citizens of Israel. “This is a democratic election,” he said. “It’s the only thing where we’re equal with the Jews. The only thing.
“When we came and expressed our dissatisfaction with this government, the Arab vote became a danger to the state,” said Siksik. “It’s not normal.”
Many Palestinian citizens of Israel believe they’ve been allowed to remain out of necessity, not equality. “The bus drivers are Arabs, the doctors in the hospitals are Arabs, the construction workers are Arabs,” Siksik notes.
But even those “essential worker” roles are being stripped away. After October 7, Israel revoked tens of thousands of work permits for Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank to enter Israel, and the essential jobs they filled are being replaced by short-term labourers brought from abroad. Yassin notes fabricated stories over the summer on Israeli social media that Arab doctors were poisoning Jewish patients at Rambam Hospital in Haifa.
“If they could give up on anything Arab, they would,” says Yassin. “It’s not because they like us [that they let us remain]… It’s not because they want to; it’s because they have to.”
Yassin herself went through that struggle for acceptance in Israeli society. After growing up in Arrabeh, she learned Hebrew so well at Ben-Gurion University that “no one knew I was an Arab any more.” She took a job at a regional council near Jerusalem, in an entirely Jewish workplace, to prove she was “fully Israeli”.
“I did not speak Arabic in public. I even voted for [left-wing Zionist party] Meretz and favoured them over Arab parties,” said Yassin. “I wanted to be ‘the good Israeli’.”
But she could never escape that sense of otherness. At the council, colleagues asked if they could call Yassin – whose first name, Lama, means “why” in Hebrew – “Yasmine” instead, because she reminded them of Jasmine from the movie Aladdin. She was Yasmine for a year and a half. “It was another demand of giving up on another part of my identity – one that defines me literally.”
And then, the Sunday after the October 7 attacks, her colleagues would not say hello back to her.
She came to realise that “shared society cannot be built over inequality.”
After becoming director of public policy at the Abraham Initiatives, which advances the rights of Palestinian citizens in Israel, Yassin testified at Knesset committee meetings regarding unchecked crime and violence affecting their communities. She describes being dismissed or silenced outright, despite prior approval to speak. “If you say one more word,” she recalled the National Security committee chairman saying, “I will ask you to leave.”
Yassin sees that derision of a Palestinian political voice carrying over into the rhetoric – and investigations – surrounding the post-election talks. In Jaffa, that wider climate was felt on November 3, when, about midnight, about 15 security officers, a few of them masked, raided the Jaffa home of Abed Abou Shehadeh, a journalist and activist, arresting him in front of his two children. Accused of having “contacts with a foreign agent”, a court has ordered him held until November 8.
In the south, meanwhile, police arrested seven Bedouin men on suspicion of planning to pay people to vote for Ra’am, which calls them party activists and denies the allegations. Arab political leader Ayman Odeh now faces investigations as well by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is run by the Netanyahu-aligned David Zini, over allegations that he received money from foreign sources to influence voter turnout. Odeh denies the allegations, calling them “political persecution”.
“We are now facing the whole Israeli system,” says Abu Rass. “I think we are facing the deep state also.”
Before the election, Abu Rass had predicted to Al Jazeera that 15 to 17 seats would have Israeli party leaders knocking on the Arab parties’ doors. But despite the Arab parties exceeding even those high expectations, that success has not yet borne such fruit.
